name_en: Helapa (Kurakkan Sweet Wrapped in Kenda Leaf)

ingredients.name: Kurakkan flour (finger millet flour)
ingredients.notes: approx. 1 cup; sieve before use for a finer dough

ingredients.name: Kithul treacle
ingredients.notes: can substitute sugar syrup, coconut treacle, jaggery (melted), or date paste

ingredients.name: All-purpose flour
ingredients.notes: approx. 1/4 cup; helps bind the dough and keep it soft

ingredients.name: Fresh kenda leaves
ingredients.notes: washed and dried; banana leaf or foil can substitute if unavailable, though flavour will differ

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: added gradually, about 1/4 to 1/2 cup total, just enough for a soft moldable dough

steps.instruction: In a medium-sized bowl, add the kurakkan flour, scraped coconut, kithul treacle, all-purpose flour, sugar, crushed cardamom, and salt.

Mix well, adding water a little at a time, until a smooth dough forms. The dough should be a little wet and sticky -- if too dry, add a touch more treacle or water; if too wet, add a little more flour.
Divide the dough into about 6-7 small portions.
Wash and dry the kenda leaves. Place one portion of dough onto each leaf and flatten it gently on one side only, leaving a small border around the edges.
Fold each leaf in half over the dough and press down firmly to seal. Trim away any dough that spills out of the edges.
Place the wrapped leaves into a steamer and steam for 15-20 minutes, until firm.
Let cool to room temperature before unwrapping. Serve with a cup of plain Ceylon tea.

source_site: thefoodsnaps.com, cross-checked against shankiikitchen.wordpress.com and peckishme.com for method consistency
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 3 independent sources; this version uses treacle as in the primary source, with jaggery noted as the traditional substitute matching the dish's classic description
notes: Helapa (also spelled Halapa) is a rural Sinhala village sweet, historically associated with Hambantota district where kurakkan (finger millet) is most commonly grown. The dish exists in two styles: dough mixed throughout with the sweetener (used here, the simpler method), or dough wrapped around a separate sweet coconut-treacle filling called 'pani pol' (a more traditional but fiddlier method). Kenda leaf (Macaranga peltata) is essential to the dish's signature aroma; banana leaf or foil are workable substitutes but change the flavour profile noticeably. Jaggery can directly replace the kithul treacle if preferred, melted slightly before mixing in.
